name: The Sagan Standard
meaning: The further a claim departs from what is already well established, the stronger and more reliable the evidence needed before it should be accepted. Ordinary claims can rest on ordinary evidence; a claim that overturns a large body of prior knowledge demands proportionally more.
mechanism: In Bayesian terms, a claim that conflicts with well-supported knowledge starts with a low prior probability, and only evidence with a very high likelihood ratio — far more probable under the extraordinary hypothesis than under mundane alternatives like error, fraud, or coincidence — can raise a low prior to a high posterior. Weak or ambiguous evidence barely moves it. So the strangeness of the claim sets the bar for the proof.

examples.text: The claim that UFOs are alien spacecraft contradicts known physics and has no corroborated physical evidence; blurry photos and eyewitness reports are ordinary-grade evidence, far short of what such an extraordinary conclusion would require. Sagan applied the standard to exactly this.

The 1989 Fleischmann–Pons claim of room-temperature nuclear fusion contradicted established nuclear physics; when independent laboratories could not replicate it, the evidence never rose to the extraordinary level the claim demanded.

The oldest form of the idea, from Hume: a reported violation of natural law requires testimony whose falsehood would itself be more improbable than the miracle — otherwise the mundane explanation wins.

variants.name: Truzzi's version
variants.text: The sociologist Marcello Truzzi's mid-1970s phrasing, 'an extraordinary claim requires extraordinary proof', which Sagan's line closely echoes.

variants.name: Laplace's principle
variants.text: Pierre-Simon Laplace, early 1800s: 'the more extraordinary the event, the greater the need of its being supported by strong proofs' — the same idea, more than a century earlier.

variants.name: Hitchens's razor
variants.text: The dismissive corollary: what can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence — the flip side of demanding proof proportional to the claim.

whyItMatters: It is the working motto of scientific scepticism: it calibrates belief to prior plausibility, so a surprising result is neither dismissed out of hand nor accepted on thin support. It is the standard by which fringe claims, from ESP to miracle cures, are weighed.

working.lead: Scale the evidence to the implausibility
working.text: the more a claim would overturn, the stronger and more independent the evidence you should demand before believing it.
error, fraud, coincidence, and misperception are the ordinary explanations that must be excluded before an extraordinary one earns consideration.
for a claim that breaks with established knowledge, independent confirmation is what turns a startling result into a credible one.

limits: The standard's weak point, conceded even by its users, is that 'extraordinary' is undefined and subjective — there is no metric for what makes either a claim or its evidence extraordinary. Applied unevenly it can entrench orthodoxy, letting people demand extraordinary proof for claims that contradict consensus while waving through consensus-friendly claims on weaker evidence, and it can set an unfairly high bar that dismisses genuine but surprising anomalies. It is a disciplined heuristic, not a formula.
misreadings: It does not say surprising claims are false, only that they carry a heavier burden of proof. Nor does it license rejecting anything that challenges consensus — the demand is for proportionate evidence, not for the claim to be impossible.
origin: Popularised by the astronomer Carl Sagan, who used the phrasing in the 1980 television series Cosmos (and in his 1979 book Broca's Brain). It has clear antecedents — Marcello Truzzi's mid-1970s 'extraordinary proof' formulation, Laplace in the early nineteenth century, and Hume's 1748 essay 'Of Miracles'. Who first attached the name 'Sagan standard' to it is not documented.

sources.text: Sagan, C. (1980). Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, episode 12. — the phrase's popular source.
"Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," Wikipedia. — the Sagan/Truzzi/Laplace/Hume lineage and the critique of the undefined 'extraordinary'.
"Extraordinary Claims Require Extraordinary Evidence." Quote Investigator (2021). — the dated history back through Truzzi and Laplace.
